opus-5.5.text:
I think the first question isn't really "should we do pre-training," it's "what is our actual moat, and does pre-training strengthen it or distract from it?"

For a company like Cursor, the biggest asset isn't the model. It's the product surface and the data that flows through it: millions of developers editing code, accepting or rejecting suggestions, iterating with agents. That's an interaction signal the big labs don't have in that form. So if I were in that seat, I'd ask: where does that signal create the most leverage?

My intuition is that it's much more valuable in post-training, reinforcement learning, and building environments and reward signals around real coding workflows, than in pre-training from scratch. Pre-training is extremely capital-intensive, and you're competing head-on with labs that have far more compute and a multi-year head start. Even if you build a decent base model, the frontier keeps moving, and you may spend a year and a lot of money to end up roughly where an open-weight model already is.

That said, I wouldn't make it a permanent no. There are a few conditions where it starts to make sense. One is if you find the base models you can access are bottlenecking you: they lack some capability that matters for your product, and it can't be fixed in post-training. Another is if dependence on a few model providers becomes a real strategic risk, on price, access, or because those providers are building competing products. A third is if your proprietary data is so large and so different that it actually changes what the base model learns, not just how it behaves.

So my practical answer would be to sequence it. First, push very hard on mid-training and RL on top of strong open models, and build the infrastructure and team that understands training deeply. That's useful regardless. Then keep evaluating: is the ceiling coming from the base model or from everything around it? If you repeatedly hit the base-model ceiling, and you have the capital and talent, then pre-training becomes a reasonable bet rather than a vanity project.

The deeper point is that in this era, product companies and model companies are converging. The question isn't whether you're "a model company." It's whether you control the parts of the stack that actually determine the user's experience. For coding agents right now, I think that's more the environment, the feedback loop, and the RL than raw pre-training.

r001.rationale: The response compares a potential Cursor base model with frontier labs and open-weight models, but does not identify the performance gap between open-source and closed-source coding models as a decision factor.

r002.rationale: The response does not assess how much of an open-source versus closed-source performance gap Cursor could close.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a hard question, and honestly I think the right answer depends less on the technology and more on what kind of company you believe you are.

If I were Cursor's CEO, the first thing I'd ask is: what's the actual bottleneck for our product? Right now the value Cursor delivers is mostly about the environment, the context, the interaction loop between the model and the codebase. A lot of that is engineering and product, not pre-training. If the frontier labs keep shipping better models every few months and you can plug them in, then spending hundreds of millions on pre-training your own base model just so you can be a year behind them is a bad trade. You'd be burning the thing you're best at, which is iteration speed on the product, to compete on the thing they're best at.

But there's a counterargument that I take seriously. If the model providers are also your competitors, and they all have coding agents now, then your dependence on them is strategic risk. They see your traffic, they can price you out, they can withhold the best model. So the question becomes: do you need to own the model, or do you need to own enough of the model?

And I think the answer for most application companies is the second one. You don't start with pre-training from scratch. You start with post-training. You have something nobody else has, which is a huge amount of real data about how people actually write code with an agent, where it fails, what gets accepted, what gets reverted. That's a reinforcement learning signal, and it's extremely valuable. You can take an open base model, or a licensed one, and make it meaningfully better at your specific task with that data. Cursor already does some of this with their tab model, and that's the right place to begin.

Then you watch two things. One, does the gap between what you can do with post-training and what the frontier does keep shrinking or widening? If open models stay within reach of the frontier, you may never need to pre-train. Two, does your scale justify it? Pre-training only makes sense when your volume is large enough that the marginal cost per token of owning the model beats renting, and when you have enough compute talent to not waste the money.

So the decision isn't a yes or no at one point in time. It's a ladder. Post-training first, then mid-training or continued pre-training on code if the economics work, and full pre-training only if you've become big enough that you're essentially a lab anyway. If I were CEO I'd be very reluctant to skip steps, because the graveyard is full of companies that decided they needed to be a foundation model company before they'd finished being a product company.

r001.rationale: The response compares open models with frontier models and says their relative performance is a factor in whether pre-training is needed.

r002.rationale: It asks whether post-training can close the gap with frontier models and whether that gap is shrinking or widening.

astra-6.text:
If I were Cursor’s CEO, I’d start with the bottleneck in the product. Where are users getting stuck, and is that something we can solve with better context, tools, or post-training? Or does it actually require a different base model?

I’d distinguish owning models from doing pre-training from scratch. You might get a lot of value from training a model for a specific part of the workflow—predicting edits, for example—without taking on the cost of building a general-purpose foundation model. I’d pursue that first and use it to learn whether our data and training work translate into a better user experience.

The question for pre-training is: what advantage does Cursor have that a model provider doesn’t? Being close to the user could give you a better understanding of real coding tasks and, with appropriate permissions, useful feedback about which changes actually work. But that doesn’t automatically mean pre-training is the best way to use that advantage.

So my default would be to keep the option open, build a strong team around evaluations and post-training, and set a concrete threshold. If we can identify an important limitation that existing models consistently fail to address, and experiments show that pre-training can fix it at a reasonable cost, then I’d invest. I wouldn’t do it simply because other companies are doing it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limitations of existing models generally, but does not identify the performance gap between open-source and closed-source coding models.

r002.rationale: It says to test whether pre-training can address a limitation, but does not identify how much of the open-source/closed-source performance gap Cursor could close.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with the question: what is the bottleneck for Cursor’s product, and does pre-training actually address it? Owning a model is a means to an end. The goal is to make developers more productive.

For example, if the biggest problems are understanding a large codebase, getting the right context, or running a long task reliably, there may be a lot you can do with retrieval, tools, and post-training. I’d want to explore those first, because they also help you understand what capabilities you actually need from the underlying model.

Then I’d ask whether Cursor has an advantage that makes pre-training worthwhile. You have this interaction with developers: what they accept, what they reject, how they revise something, whether the code eventually works. The question is whether you can turn that feedback into a learning signal that produces a substantially better coding model. Having usage alone doesn’t automatically give you that.

I would probably build a small research effort and test the hypothesis before committing a huge amount of compute. Can we produce a model that makes the product meaningfully better on real developer tasks, at a reasonable cost and latency? And does that advantage persist as the external models improve?

If the answer is yes, I’d scale it. If not, I’d be comfortable continuing to use other people’s models. You can build a very valuable product without doing every layer yourself.

r001.rationale: The response weighs its model against external models generally, but does not identify the open-source versus closed-source coding-model performance gap as a decision factor.

r002.rationale: It asks whether Cursor can build a meaningfully better model, but does not address how much of the open-source/closed-source performance gap Cursor could close.
